title.narrative: Mapping Mental Health Resources for Young People Living in a Conflict Con-text at The Colombian Pacific Region

description.narrative: Deliver significant research funding for internationally competitive and innovative collaborative projects between researchers from Colombia and United Kingdom that will allow the pursuit of shared research interests. The ODA statements says: The social integration of those who have had a direct or indirect role in the conflict is a perpetual problem across conflict-affected countries and mental health is a critical element of this. Those suffering from trauma and mental health issues following conflict are frequently ostracised, making reintegration even more difficult. Without reintegration, conflict experienced adults and their families including children, and conflict experienced adolescents face marginalisation within communities. This impacts upon their ability to engage in employment and exacerbates loneliness, isolation, poor mental health and poverty. We need to understand the needs of conflict-affected young people, within a context of practically and fiscally constrained public services and grassroots community resources, in order to successfully guide policy to interrupt the generational mental health legacy of the conflict. In Colombia the conflict in both rural and urban areas has resulted in a generational legacy of poor mental health. Many communities who have direct or indirect experience of conflict and have experienced trauma have little or no access to medical or other community mental health services. We do not sufficiently understand how experience of conflict shapes young people’s identity and impacts upon their mental health. Reintegration and the mental health of conflict experienced young people is little researched. In Colombia’s current reincorporation process of former FARC combatants, no mental health strategy is implemented. Although the reparation process for survivors does contain elements of psychosocial support, according to an evaluation carried out by Harvard’s Carr Centre (Sikkink et al, 2015), these are relatively short-term and with a limited focus, their effectiveness for the millions of victims has not yet been proven. The 2015 National Mental Health Survey (ENMS) identified that alcohol consumption linked to exposure to traumatic events and violence, was one of the main effects of mental health problems among young people in Colombia. The survey highlighted that almost 30% of Colombian adolescents had experienced a traumatic event, oftentimes related to the conflict, especially forced displacement. The ENMS identified that psychological symptoms as a result of traumatic events tended to be stronger among young women. Better mental health support services for young people are crucial to make sure that young people, in a pivotal phase of their mental and physical development, can break through the effects of trauma and substance abuse interrupting the cycle of violence, and achieve their potential. The participatory and creative methods proposed in this project enable a discussion with young people on their own terms to better identify what contributes to or diminishes their mental health, and how young people can be more effectively supported. The ENMS also indicated that the main challenges to improving mental health were the need to strengthen the quality and accessibility of mental health support services, especially primary access at the community level. Additionally, the ENMS indicated that changing attitudes that prevent people from accessing those services, as a result of (auto) stigmatisation, should be a priority. The present research offers a unique opportunity to further those goals, by identifying the main challenges for young people’s mental health care, as well as determining what services are available to them at the national and community level, and how those can be improved. This research will map mental health patterns very widely, also showing how community practices can be incorporated into health provision (or not). As such it involves practical lessons for other communities undergoing similar transitions from conflict to peace, thus benefiting more than half of the least developed countries on the DAC list.
The fund addresses the UN sustainable development goals. It aims to maximise the impact of research and innovation to improve lives and opportunity in the developing world
